<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
Use this page when your outcome is a cost: healthcare costs, lost earnings or
both, summed per person over follow-up. It covers the analysis side: what to
estimate, how to describe costs, which models fit them, how to handle censoring
and uncertainty, and how to bring costs to one price year. Where the cost of
each hospital contact, prescription or service comes from is in [Healthcare
costs](register-reference.qmd#healthcare-costs-under-development) under
Overview of registers.

You start from an analysis dataset with one row per person (or per person and
year), a cost in DKK, follow-up time, exposure and covariates ([Phase
12](data-manipulation.qmd)). You end with mean costs per group and an excess
cost with a confidence interval.

::: {.callout-warning title="Structural guidance, not verified code"}
The code on this page shows the shape of each step. It has **not been run on
register data**. Check the column names against your own dataset, and the
choices against your analysis plan.
:::

*Variable names in the examples are generic. Replace them with your own.* The
models use `glm()` from base R and `dplyr` for data handling.

## Start from the estimand {#estimand}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
Decide what number you want before you choose a model.

- **Mean cost per person over a fixed horizon**, for example the five years
  after the index date. A person who dies contributes the costs up to death and
  nothing after.
- **Mean cost per person-year**: the summed costs divided by the summed
  person-years at risk, in the same way as a rate (see [Rates and rate ratios
  (Poisson)](rates-poisson.qmd)).
- **Total cost or excess cost.** The total cost is what the exposed group
  costs. The excess cost (also called attributable or incremental cost) is the
  difference between the mean cost of the exposed and the mean cost of
  comparable unexposed people. Excess cost needs a comparison group.

The comparison group is built in the same way as for any other outcome:

- **Matched controls**: [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd).
- **Weighting**: [IP weighting (IPTW)](weighting-iptw.qmd).
- **Regression standardisation** (the g-formula): fit a cost model, predict the
  cost for everyone as exposed and as unexposed, and average the two
  predictions. The fold-out on standardisation in [IP
  weighting](weighting-iptw.qmd) explains the idea, and the [two-part
  model](#two-part) below shows it for costs.

**Report the mean, not only the median.** In a skewed distribution the median
is lower than the mean, and it cannot be multiplied up to a total. Barber and
Thompson write that analysis of costs "needs to focus on arithmetic mean
costs, since these will reflect the total cost of treating all patients with
the disease" ([Barber & Thompson
2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11113956/)). Mihaylova et al. make the
same point for policy makers ([Mihaylova et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653)). Medians and quartiles are still
useful to describe the distribution.

## Describe the costs first {#describe}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
Look at the distribution before you fit anything. Cost data are non-negative,
usually strongly skewed to the right, often have many zeros (people with no
contact in the period) and can have heavy tails ([Mihaylova et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653)).

Per group, report the number of people, person-years, the share with zero
cost, the mean with its standard deviation, the median and quartiles, and the
total by cost domain (hospital, primary care, medication).

```r
library(dplyr) # group_by, summarise

df %>%
  group_by(exposure) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    person_years = sum(follow_up_years),
    share_zero = mean(cost == 0),     # share of people with no cost at all
    mean_cost = mean(cost),
    sd_cost = sd(cost),
    median_cost = median(cost),
    q1 = quantile(cost, 0.25),
    q3 = quantile(cost, 0.75),
    total_cost = sum(cost)
  )
```

The very large values are part of the mean you want to estimate, so removing
or capping them changes what the mean describes. A maximum is one person's
value, and a median or percentile in a small group can be too, so check them
against the export rules before they leave DST (see
[Export](export.qmd#min-max-median)).

## Choosing a model {#models}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
In a large cohort you may not need a model for the crude comparison. In a
review aimed at trials, Mihaylova et al. recommend simple methods "in large
samples where the near-normality of sample means is assured" ([Mihaylova et
al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653)), such as a difference in means
with a normal-based confidence interval. Barber and Thompson recommend the
bootstrap as a check on such methods, or as the main analysis for moderately
sized samples of skewed costs ([Barber & Thompson
2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11113956/)). A model is needed when you
adjust or standardise, and then the skewness and the zeros matter.

### Why not linear regression on log costs {#log-ols}

Taking the log of the cost and fitting `lm()` gives coefficients on the log
scale, and `exp()` of a predicted log cost is not the mean cost. Getting back
to DKK needs a retransformation. Duan's smearing factor does this when the
log-scale error has constant variance. When the variance differs with the
covariates, as it often does, the simple retransformation is biased, and a
correct one is cumbersome ([Manning & Mullahy
2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11469231/); [Manning et al.
2005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2004.09.011)). The log is also
undefined at zero, and adding a constant to the zeros is not recommended
([Mihaylova et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653)).

### GLM with a log link {#glm-log}

A generalised linear model with a log link models the mean cost on the DKK
scale directly: the predicted mean is exp(xβ), with no smearing factor.
`exp()` of a coefficient is a ratio of mean costs. A difference in DKK comes from standardisation, as in
the [two-part model](#two-part) below.

The variance function (the GLM family) says how the variance grows with the
mean. The estimate of the mean is usually robust to a wrong variance function,
but the precision is not ([Mihaylova et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653)). Manning and Mullahy write the
variance as a power of the mean, var(y | x) proportional to E(y | x)^λ, and
propose a Park-type test to estimate λ: regress the log of the squared
raw-scale residual on the log of the predicted mean, and read off the slope
([Manning & Mullahy 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11469231/); called
a modified Park test in [Manning et al.
2005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhealeco.2004.09.011)).

  | Slope λ near | Variance                 | `family =` in `glm()`            |
  | ------------ | ------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
  | 0            | constant                 | `gaussian(link = "log")`         |
  | 1            | proportional to the mean | `quasipoisson(link = "log")`     |
  | 2            | mean squared             | `Gamma(link = "log")`            |
  | 3            | mean cubed               | `inverse.gaussian(link = "log")` |

```r
library(dplyr) # filter

pos <- filter(df, cost > 0)                          # people with any cost
fit <- glm(cost ~ exposure + age + sex, data = pos,
           family = Gamma(link = "log"))             # a first GLM with log link

res <- residuals(fit, type = "response")             # raw-scale residual: cost minus predicted mean
park <- lm(log(res^2) ~ log(fitted(fit)))            # log squared residual on log predicted mean
coef(park)[2]                                        # the slope: an estimate of lambda
```

Manning and Mullahy also check the residuals from a model for log cost first:
if they are heavy-tailed, linear regression on log cost with a careful
retransformation can be the more precise choice. In their simulations the
test was less informative when the data were heavy-tailed. When the family is
picked this way, they recommend robust or bootstrapped standard errors,
because the estimated variance function may still be wrong ([Manning & Mullahy
2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11469231/)).

### Two-part model for costs with many zeros {#two-part}

When many people have no cost, a two-part model fits the zeros and the
positive costs separately ([Belotti et al.
2015](https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X1501500102)):

1. A logistic regression for the probability of any cost.
2. A GLM with a log link for the cost among those with any cost.

The mean cost is the product of the two parts: E(cost | x) = Pr(cost > 0 | x)
× E(cost | cost > 0, x) ([Belotti et al.
2015](https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X1501500102)). In the review by
Mihaylova et al., two-part models "seem to outperform other methods when
excess zeros are present". Hurdle models are the counterpart for counts, such
as the number of contacts, not for costs in DKK ([Belotti et al.
2015](https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X1501500102)).

The sketch fits both parts and standardises: it predicts each person's mean
cost as exposed and as unexposed, and the excess cost is the difference of the
two averages. `exposure` is 0/1 here. If it is a factor, set the levels in
`mutate()` instead.

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, mutate

df <- readRDS("path/to/cost_analysis.rds") # one row per person: cost over the horizon (DKK), exposure 0/1, covariates

excess_cost <- function(d) {
  part1 <- glm(I(cost > 0) ~ exposure + age + sex,     # part 1: Pr(any cost)
               data = d, family = binomial)
  part2 <- glm(cost ~ exposure + age + sex,             # part 2: mean cost among those with any cost
               data = filter(d, cost > 0), family = Gamma(link = "log"))

  mean_cost_if <- function(e) {
    d_e <- mutate(d, exposure = e)                      # everyone exposed (1) or everyone unexposed (0)
    predict(part1, d_e, type = "response") *            # Pr(cost > 0) ...
      predict(part2, d_e, type = "response")            # ... times E(cost | cost > 0)
  }

  mean(mean_cost_if(1)) - mean(mean_cost_if(0))         # excess mean cost per person, DKK
}

excess_cost(df)
```

The standardised means are averages over everyone in `df`, so the excess cost
is for the whole cohort. To get it for the exposed only, average over the
exposed rows. The function returns a single number, so the confidence interval
comes from the bootstrap below. [Liu et al.
2019](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8140) show how to split an effect on the
mean cost into its effect on the probability of any cost and on the cost among
users.

## Censored costs {#censoring}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
For mean cost per person over a fixed horizon, death ends the costs: it is not
censoring. Emigration and the end of your data are censoring, because the costs
after that date are unknown. Migration dates come from [VNDS](register-reference.qmd#vnds---migration-register).

Lin et al. write that "the naive sample average of the observed costs from all
study subjects or from the uncensored cases only can be severely biased, and
the standard survival analysis techniques are not applicable" ([Lin et al.
1997](https://doi.org/10.2307/2533947)). Kaplan-Meier with cost in place of
time fails because the cost accumulated up to censoring is not independent of
the cost up to death ([Wijeysundera et al.
2012](https://doi.org/10.2147/CEOR.S31552)). Two estimators were developed for
this:

- **Lin et al. (1997)** split follow-up into intervals, take the mean cost in
  each interval among those alive at its start, and weight it by the
  Kaplan-Meier probability of being alive at the start
  ([Lin et al. 1997](https://doi.org/10.2307/2533947)).
- **Bang and Tsiatis (2000)** weight each person with complete follow-up by
  the inverse of the probability of remaining uncensored, which allows
  censoring at any time ([Bang & Tsiatis
  2000](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/87.2.329)). The partitioned version also
  uses the costs a censored person had in the periods before censoring. It
  needs cost per period, which register data give ([Wijeysundera et al.
  2012](https://doi.org/10.2147/CEOR.S31552)).

Both assume that censoring is independent of future costs. Wijeysundera et al.
give a worked example for readers without an advanced statistical background,
cite simulations in which the simple weighted estimator became unstable with
more than 50% censoring, and describe phase-based costing as an alternative
when censoring is heavy ([Wijeysundera et al.
2012](https://doi.org/10.2147/CEOR.S31552)). The weighting idea is the same as
IPCW in [IP weighting](weighting-iptw.qmd), with a weight that depends on
each person's follow-up time.

With mean cost per person-year, a person who emigrates contributes the costs and
the person-years observed before the date, as with a rate.

## Uncertainty: bootstrap {#bootstrap}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
The non-parametric bootstrap gives a confidence interval for a difference in
mean costs without assuming normality ([Barber & Thompson
2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11113956/)). For a model-based estimate
such as the two-part model above, repeat the whole procedure in each bootstrap
sample: both models and the standardisation, and the weights too if you
weighted.

Resample the unit that the rows depend on:

- **The person**, when a person has several rows (one per year, or matched
  more than once). This is the same reason as for [clustered standard
  errors](regression.qmd#clustered-standard-errors).
- **The matched set**, in a matched cohort. For propensity-score matched pairs,
  resampling the pairs gave standard errors close to the true sampling
  variation in simulations ([Austin & Small
  2014](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6276)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Code: bootstrap the excess cost by person"}
```r
library(dplyr) # inner_join

set.seed(2026)
ids <- unique(df$pnr)                                    # use match_id instead to resample matched sets

boot <- replicate(1000, {
  draw <- data.frame(pnr = sample(ids, replace = TRUE))  # draw persons, not rows
  d_b <- inner_join(draw, df, by = "pnr",
                    relationship = "many-to-many")       # all rows of each drawn person, once per draw
  excess_cost(d_b)                                       # the function from the two-part model above
})

quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))                          # percentile 95% interval
```

Each replicate refits both models on the whole cohort, so time a few
replicates before you start a thousand. The percentile interval is the
simplest. Barber and Thompson preferred the bootstrap-t and the bias-corrected
and accelerated (BCa) intervals ([Barber & Thompson
2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11113956/)).
:::

## Prices: bring all costs to one price year {#price-year}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
A cost from 2012 is in 2012 prices, and a cost from 2024 in 2024 prices. Before
you sum or compare across years, convert every cost to one price year with a
price index:

> cost in price year B = cost in year t × index(B) / index(t)

Two Danish indices:

- **The consumer price index** from DST. Annual averages are in StatBank table
  [PRIS8](https://www.statbank.dk/PRIS8) (from 1900), and the monthly index in
  [PRIS01](https://www.statbank.dk/PRIS01). Older papers cite table PRIS111,
  which DST no longer updates: its last month is December 2025.
- **The Danish Regions' price and wage development for health care**,
  "Sundheds-PL ekskl. medicintilskud". It is published as a yearly percentage
  change. Each year's note gives the final figure for the year before and
  estimates for the next two ([Pris- og lønreguleringen 2025-27, June
  2026](https://www.regioner.dk/media/3tnlfxqa/pris-og-loenreguleringen-2025-27.pdf)).
  To use it as an index, chain the yearly changes.

DRG tariffs are computed each year (see [Healthcare
costs](register-reference.qmd#healthcare-costs-under-development)), so hospital
costs priced with tariffs from several years need the same conversion.

## Discounting {#discounting}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
Discounting converts costs that fall in later years to their value in a start
year. It is a separate step from the price index: first bring costs to one
price year, then discount.

The Danish Ministry of Finance recommends a real discount rate of 3.5% a year
for years 0-35, 2.5% for years 36-70 and 1.5% after year 70 ([Vejledning i
samfundsøkonomiske konsekvensvurderinger, June
2023](https://fm.dk/media/27314/vejledning-i-samfundsoekonomiske-konsekvensvurderinger-juni-2023_web-a.pdf),
section 4.7, table 4.1). The rate in force is kept in the Ministry's key
figures catalogue, which in June 2026 gives the same rates
([Nøgletalskatalog, June
2026](https://fm.dk/media/4tkj2o4w/noegletalskatalog_juni-2026.pdf)). Until
January 2021 the rates were 4%, 3% and 2% (Vejledning 2023, preface). The
guidance says the rate will be adjusted in the catalogue when the Ministry's
assumptions about the real interest rate change for good.

In the Ministry's worked example the value in year 0 is not discounted. For
horizons under 35 years each later year is divided by 1.035 once more:

```r
library(dplyr) # mutate

# year_since_start: 0 for the first year of follow-up, 1 for the next, ...
costs_by_year <- costs_by_year %>%
  mutate(cost_discounted = cost_real / 1.035^year_since_start) # cost_real: cost in one price year
```

## Productivity costs {#productivity}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
A societal cost study can add lost production to healthcare costs. Two
methods value it differently. The human capital method "counts any hour not
worked as an hour lost". The friction cost method "only counts as lost those
hours not worked until another employee takes over the patient's work", and the
two can give widely different results ([van den Hout
2010](https://doi.org/10.1136/ard.2009.117150); the friction cost method is
from [Koopmanschap et al. 1995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10154656/)).

Registers at DST that carry the inputs:

- **IND** (Indkomst), yearly from 1980, holds personal income. `LOENMV_13` is
  wage income ("Lønindkomst i alt") and includes pay during sickness and
  parental leave. `ERHVERVSINDK_13` is wage income plus net income from
  self-employment ([DST, IND variable
  list](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/IND%20-%20Indkomst.html);
  [DST, LOENMV_13](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/generelt-om-data/dokumentation-af-data/hoejkvalitetsvariable/personindkomster/loenmv-13)).
- **AKM** gives the main labour-market status per year (see [Employment -
  AKM](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#employment)).
- **DREAM**, a database of public benefit spells, gives the type of benefit
  week by week for each person who received one, such as sickness benefit or
  unemployment benefit ([DREAM vejledning, version
  51](https://aku.dst.dk/ext/36881106234/0/forskning/DREAM-Manual-Version-51--pdf)).

FAIK, used in this guide for SEPLINE's income measure, is household-equivalised
disposable income ([FAIK](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income)), not a
person's earnings.

None of these registers records time spent caring for a relative. A Danish
study of informal care for people with dementia collected care time in a
postal survey of caregivers, and the value per day depended on the method.
With care time valued at a professional caregiver's wage (the proxy good
method) it was EUR 160-223 per day for the primary caregiver. Counting only
weekday care by caregivers in the labour market, valued as lost production, it
was EUR 35-45 ([Jakobsen et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1159/000333812)).

## What to report {#report}

<!-- TODO(Sara): wording -->
Each choice on this page changes the number, so a reader needs all of them to
interpret the estimate and compare it with other studies:

- The estimand: per person or per person-year, horizon, total or excess, and
  the comparison group.
- The cost domains included and the source of each unit cost (see [Healthcare
  costs](register-reference.qmd#healthcare-costs-under-development)).
- How zeros, very large values, death and censoring were handled.
- The model: family and link, how you chose them, and the result with another
  family.
- The uncertainty method and the unit you resampled.
- The price year and the price index, and the discount rate with year 0.
- Mean costs per group in DKK, the excess cost with its confidence interval,
  and the share with zero cost.

For a guide to how cost-of-illness studies are read and judged, see [Larg & Moss 2011](https://doi.org/10.2165/11588380-000000000-00000).

::: {.callout-tip title="Read more"}
- [Mihaylova et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653): review of
  statistical methods for costs, with a summary table of what each handles.
- [Manning & Mullahy 2001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11469231/): log
  models, GLMs and the Park test.
- [Wijeysundera et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.2147/CEOR.S31552): censored
  costs explained for health services researchers, with a worked example.
- [Barber & Thompson 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11113956/): the
  bootstrap for mean costs.
- [Healthcare costs](register-reference.qmd#healthcare-costs-under-development):
  where the unit costs come from.
:::
